case_title: Satya Narayana Tiwari and Anr v. State of U.P.
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband of the victim); Relative (mother-in-law of the victim)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B; IPC s.498-A; Dowry Prohibition Act 1961 s.4
weapon: Half-burnt cloth with a knot (ligature) used for strangulation; kerosene used for burning
evidence_type: Circumstantial; medical (post mortem report); recovery memos (blood and bindi, broken bangles, burnt phone); testimony of the victim's father and a relative on dowry demand; false police report as conduct evidence
aggravating_circumstances: Death by strangulation followed by burning; persistent dowry demand for a Maruti car; deliberate false report to police claiming suicide to mislead the investigation; pre-planning by the accused
high_court_outcome: Convictions under IPC s.304-B, s.498-A and DPA s.4 upheld as sentenced: life for s.304-B, 3 years RI for s.498-A, 6 months RI for s.4 DPA, concurrent
offence_finally_established: Dowry death under IPC s.304-B; cruelty under IPC s.498-A; Dowry Prohibition Act s.4
neutral_facts: A married woman aged about 24 was found dead in the bedroom of her matrimonial home about three years after her marriage. Her death was caused by strangulation and burning. The victim's father alleged that after about six months of marriage the accused, her husband and mother-in-law, repeatedly demanded a Maruti car as dowry. He stated that the victim told him of being tortured and maltreated for non-fulfilment of the demand, both over the telephone and on visits to her parental home. About three months before the death, the father and a relative went to the matrimonial home to try to resolve the matter. They were humiliated and told not to return without meeting the demand. The post mortem by a panel of three doctors recorded a ligature mark about 31 by 7 centimetres around the neck, a half-burnt cloth with a knot tied around the neck, superficial to deep burns over the body, and a smell of kerosene. The cause of death was recorded as suffocation with shock from strangulation with simultaneous ante-mortem burns. Investigators recovered blood and a bloodstained bindi from a balcony outside the room, broken bangles inside the room, and a burnt cordless phone and burnt wire stuck with the body. The body was found in a corner of the bedroom. The accused claimed the death was suicide. The mother-in-law lodged a police report stating that the victim had committed suicide. Both accused were absconding for some days before the husband surrendered and then the mother-in-law did.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by strangulation and burning; ligature mark around the neck 31 x 7 cm; superficial to deep burns over the whole body; sooty particles in the air passages
number_of_offences: 3 charged (IPC s.304-B, s.498-A, DPA s.4; inferred from the convictions, as the charge list is not set out); 3 finally upheld
premeditation_planning: Yes. The court found the crime was committed with pre-planning, and the telephone call to the father and the false police report were part of a scheme to project suicide.
motive: Dowry: persistent demand for a Maruti car, not satisfied by the victim's father
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of the victim's father and a relative on the dowry demand and harassment; post mortem report and the evidence of the doctor; recovery memos (blood and bindi, bangles, burnt phone); the inquest and recovery witnesses; the investigating officer's evidence on absconding and surrender
witness_credibility: The father's and the relative's testimony was found credible and corroborative; the father was not found to act out of malice, since the other family members were not implicated. The defence sister's testimony was interested and not believed. The recoveries were not challenged in cross-examination. The court rejected the defence theory of suicide.
post_offence_conduct: Both accused absconded; the husband surrendered in court on 7.11.2000 and the mother-in-law on 13.11.2000. The mother-in-law lodged a false police report that the victim had committed suicide. The court held that absconding was not normal conduct of innocent persons.
bail_history: Bail granted by the Supreme Court on 27.10.2005; bail bonds cancelled on dismissal of the appeal
trial_duration: offence: 03.11.2000; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 12.07.2005; Supreme Court: 28.10.2010
legal_representation: Accused: Indu Malhotra, Rajesh and Vivek Jain. State: K.T.S. Tulsi, Shail Kr. Dwivedi (AAG), R.K. Gupta, Pradeep Misra, Suraj Singh, Vandana Mishra, Anurag Dubey, Meenesh Dube, Ravinder Singh and S.R. Setia
investigation_status: FIR registered on 03.11.2000; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: The trial judge treated non-production of the knot as a ground against the prosecution, though the knot had been removed during the post mortem. The court also noted that no charge under s.302 IPC was framed although the case was a murder.
appeal_history: Trial court: both accused acquitted. High Court: convicted under IPC s.304-B, s.498-A and DPA s.4, with concurrent sentences. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld.
defence_argument: The demand came about six months after marriage and there was no evidence of any demand in the three months before death, so the 'soon before' proximity test was not met (relying on Balwant). The defence also relied on the suicide theory, the alibi, an alleged manipulated post mortem report, and the claim that the victim's father received the telephone call from the accused.
legal_principle_applied: Ingredients of s.304-B IPC (Kunhiabdulla); 'soon before' as a relative term applying the proximity test; presumption under s.113-B Evidence Act; cruelty may be mental as well as physical; bride burning as rarest of rare
precedent_relied_upon: Kunhiabdulla v. State of Kerala, 2004 (4) SCC 13 (relied on; distinguished on facts in part); Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1980 SC 898 (referred to); Balwant v. State of Punjab, AIR 2005 SC 1504 (cited by defence and distinguished)
sentencing_rationale: The court held the case would have warranted death under s.302 IPC, but since no s.302 charge was framed it could not impose death. The High Court's sentence was therefore upheld, with the court noting such cases are the rarest of rare.
judicial_aggravating_factors: Bride burning is barbaric and brutal; crimes against women are social crimes calling for harsh punishment; victim was killed by strangulation then burning; deliberate false report to mislead the police
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds cancelled; accused to be taken into custody to serve the remaining sentence. The court also made general observations that dowry killings must be stamped out 'with an iron hand' (not a formal direction).
